nodes.title: Voice Agent
nodes.summary: A real-time system that listens, thinks, and speaks back in a conversation.
nodes.notes:
The A-to-Z map. Everything in this encyclopedia hangs off the pipeline stages below.

Stages: **turn detection -> STT -> LLM -> TTS -> transport**, with eval and deployment wrapped around them.

nodes.title: Voice Activity Detection
nodes.summary: Deciding when the user started and stopped speaking.
nodes.notes:
Gatekeeper of the pipeline. Bad VAD shows up as the agent talking over people or waiting too long before replying.

- Works on short audio frames and decides whether each frame contains speech. Adjacent speech frames are grouped into a segment before going downstream.
- A simple detector can use short-time energy and zero-crossing rate. Neural detectors handle messy rooms better, but cost more and can still fail on music, crosstalk and breathing.
- Quality is not just classification accuracy. In an agent, the visible failures are clipped first words, long waits, and the agent speaking over the caller.

nodes.title: Speech-to-Text
nodes.summary: Turning captured audio into text for the LLM.
nodes.notes: Selection criteria I care about: WER, real-time factor, streaming support, noise robustness.

nodes.title: Large Language Model
nodes.summary: The reasoning layer that decides what the agent says and does.
nodes.notes: For voice, time-to-first-token matters more than raw throughput; the user hears the pause.

nodes.title: Text-to-Speech
nodes.summary: Synthesising the agent's reply as audio.
nodes.notes: Streaming synthesis is what makes a reply feel instant, even when the full sentence takes longer.

nodes.title: Speech-to-Speech
nodes.summary: End-to-end models that skip the separate STT/LLM/TTS stages.
nodes.notes:
Fewer hops means lower latency and better prosody, at the cost of control over each stage.

- A cascaded agent gives a transcript, interchangeable providers and control over each stage — easier to inspect and repair.
- An end-to-end speech model can preserve tone and overlap while removing network hops, but it is harder to constrain, evaluate and debug.
- Not simply old versus new. The right choice depends on whether control or natural conversational behaviour matters more for the product.

nodes.title: Transport
nodes.summary: Moving audio between the user and the agent in real time.
nodes.notes: WebRTC for browsers and apps, SIP for phones. Transport choice sets the latency floor.

nodes.title: Telephony
nodes.summary: Connecting the agent to the phone network.
nodes.notes: Narrowband audio, jitter, and DTMF handling make phone calls harder than a browser mic.

nodes.title: Turn Taking
nodes.summary: Deciding whose turn it is to speak.
nodes.notes: End-of-turn detection is the hard part: a pause mid-thought is not the same as a finished sentence.

nodes.title: Word Error Rate
nodes.summary: Transcription accuracy measured against a reference transcript.
nodes.notes: Varies a lot by model size, accent, and language. Benchmark on your own audio, not just published numbers.

nodes.title: Real-Time Factor
nodes.summary: Processing time divided by audio duration.
nodes.notes:
Below 1.0 means faster than real time. For live agents you want a lot of headroom, not just under 1.

- Processing time divided by audio duration. Below 1 means faster than real time.
- For a live agent, merely staying below 1 is not enough. The front end needs headroom for concurrent calls, jitter and the rest of the pipeline.

nodes.title: Time to First Token
nodes.summary: How long the LLM takes to emit its first token.
nodes.notes: The metric that decides whether the agent feels snappy. Total tokens per second matters less once TTS is streaming.

nodes.title: Mean Opinion Score
nodes.summary: Human rating of synthesised speech quality.
nodes.notes:
Subjective, but still the best proxy for whether a voice sounds acceptable.

- Still the clearest answer to “would a person accept this voice?”, but slow and rater-dependent.
- Automated scores such as PESQ are useful for comparing signal degradation, not for declaring that synthetic speech sounds human.

nodes.title: Silero VAD
nodes.summary: Small neural voice activity detector.
nodes.notes: Light enough to run per-frame on CPU alongside everything else.

nodes.title: WebRTC VAD
nodes.summary: Classic signal-processing based voice activity detector.
nodes.notes: Very cheap and predictable, weaker in noisy environments than neural detectors.

nodes.title: Whisper
nodes.summary: Open-source multilingual speech recognition model family.
nodes.notes: Strong accuracy baseline. Vanilla implementation is not built for streaming.

nodes.title: Deepgram
nodes.summary: Hosted streaming speech recognition; Flux family also covers conversation-native TTS.

nodes.title: Llama 3.3 70B
nodes.summary: Open-weight instruction-tuned model used as the agent brain.
nodes.notes: What I used in the series, served through a fast hosted endpoint rather than locally.

nodes.title: Groq
nodes.summary: Low-latency hosted inference focused on open models.
nodes.notes:
- Among the **fastest** hosts for open models (with Cerebras for Gemma-class).
- Re-benchmark periodically — latency rankings drift.

nodes.title: Ollama
nodes.summary: Local model runner with a simple install and API.
nodes.notes: Easiest way to get a local LLM running while prototyping.

nodes.title: vLLM
nodes.summary: High-throughput inference engine for serving LLMs.
nodes.notes: Better fit than Ollama once you need concurrency across many calls.

nodes.title: Piper
nodes.summary: Lightweight local neural TTS.
nodes.notes: Small CPU model; good for **flow/logic testing**, not necessarily prod quality. Real cost cut vs premium hosted voices when accents pass QA.

nodes.title: XTTS-v2
nodes.summary: Open TTS model with voice cloning support.
nodes.notes: Good expressiveness and cloning, heavier than the small models.

nodes.title: ElevenLabs
nodes.summary: Hosted TTS known for natural, expressive voices.
nodes.notes:
Strong quality + voice catalog (accent/gender).

**Cost/credits** become the binding constraint at scale  plan failover early.

Keep a **hot secondary** and exercise fallback (providers do have outages).

nodes.title: Cartesia
nodes.summary: Hosted low-latency streaming TTS; also offers fast Ink STT/endpointing.
nodes.notes: Solid voices; **Ink** noted as fast for STT/endpointing.

nodes.title: OpenAI Realtime API
nodes.summary: Hosted speech-to-speech conversational API.
nodes.notes: Collapses the pipeline into one connection. Less control over individual stages.

nodes.title: Pipecat
nodes.summary: Open-source framework for real-time voice and multimodal agents.
nodes.notes: Frames flow through frame processors arranged in a pipeline. Handles interruption plumbing so you do not rebuild it.

nodes.title: LiveKit
nodes.summary: WebRTC infrastructure plus agents runtime; Cloud and self-hosted.
nodes.notes:
- **Egress/recording capacity is a hard limit**; don’t make recording-start failure fatal to the call unless required.

- Failover: parallel workers, health-check self-hosted, route **new** sessions to Cloud when saturated (in-flight may drop).

- Colocated LiveKit Inference can deliver **very low in-call TTFT** for open models.

nodes.title: WebRTC
nodes.summary: Low-latency real-time audio transport for browsers and apps.
nodes.notes: Handles jitter buffering, echo cancellation, and packet loss so you do not have to.

nodes.title: Twilio
nodes.summary: Telephony provider for connecting agents to phone calls.
nodes.notes: Media streams bridge a call into your agent over a websocket.

nodes.title: Observability
nodes.summary: Tracing, cost, latency, and eval telemetry for voice agents.
nodes.notes:
For voice stacks you need per-stage visibility: STT, turn-taking, LLM TTFT, TTS, and end-to-end TTFA — not just one aggregate latency number.

Tag every span with **provider** so cost and latency can be compared across backends.

nodes.title: Langfuse
nodes.summary: Open-source LLM observability: traces, cost, latency, scores, prompts, and datasets.
nodes.notes:
### Features
- **Tracing** — nested traces/spans for each LLM/STT/TTS step
- **Usage & cost** — per-call token usage and cost roll-ups
- **Latency** — span timings, TTFT / completion-start
- **Sessions** — group multi-turn interactions
- **Datasets** — build datasets from real traces for evaluation
- **Scores / evals** — attach LLM-as-judge or programmatic scores to traces
- **Prompt management** — versioned prompts
- **OpenTelemetry** — OTEL-compatible ingestion

### Gotchas
- Shared OTEL exporter + framework auto-instrumentation can create **orphan/duplicate traces** — isolate or filter exporters.
- Float `usage_details` may be dropped — send **integers** (e.g. `audio_duration_ms`).
- Spans that end at async drain look “instant” — backdate with real `duration_ms` / TTFT.
- Tag **provider** as a property so dashboards group by backend.
- Trace **sims + evals**, not only live calls.

nodes.title: Time to First Audio
nodes.summary: How long until the user hears the first audio from the agent.
nodes.notes:
Separate from **TTFT** (LLM). A fast model does not guarantee low TTFA — turn detection, TTS warmup, and transport all sit on the path.

Even “fast” end-to-end stacks often land around **~1–2s median**. Budget UX accordingly.

nodes.title: Cerebras
nodes.summary: Ultra-low-latency host for open models (Gemma-class, OSS).
nodes.notes:
Among the **fastest hosts** for open models.

Best fit for **latency-sensitive/ realtime** paths.

Ultra-fast hosts usually cost **more per token** than serverless clouds for the same model  pick by role, not price alone.

nodes.title: Fireworks
nodes.summary: Multi-model serverless inference host.
nodes.notes: - Multi-model serverless can be **markedly slower** than specialized fast hosts

nodes.title: MorphLLM
nodes.summary: Dedicated / fast OSS inference host.

nodes.title: Wafer.ai
nodes.summary: Latency-oriented OSS serverless inference.
nodes.notes: Positioned as **OSS-only, fast**, with zero data retention. Often cited with GLM-class models for voice stacks.

nodes.title: Baseten
nodes.summary: Inference host used as a latency reference for GLM-class models.

nodes.title: Featherless
nodes.summary: Cheap host for background AI usage where provide fixed cost per month but have concurrency limit
nodes.notes:
- **Low-tier/fixed plans throttle hard on concurrency** — batch, don’t burst. 
- suitable for background AI task

nodes.title: GCP / Vertex AI
nodes.summary: Google cloud model hosting — serverless Gemini path and Vertex endpoints.
nodes.notes:
- Serverless clouds can be **much cheaper** than fast hosts for the same open model.
- **Quotas can bite mid-session** — verify tier/TPM before prod.
- Prefer a **host abstraction** so heavier ops (endpoint, service account, secrets) aren’t a one-off code path.
- Distinguish **Vertex vs the Gemini API** — same models, different auth/quota.

nodes.title: Azure OpenAI / AI Foundry
nodes.summary: Regionized enterprise host for OpenAI and other model families.
nodes.notes:
**Not every model is in every region**; TPM/RPM vary by model + region  deploy region first.

**Provisioned throughput** reserves capacity, but **burst spillover is billed**.

Different **model families may need separate regional deployments**.

nodes.title: OpenRouter
nodes.summary: Gateway that routes one model id across many underlying hosts.
nodes.notes:
Useful to see **which hosts serve a given model** before native integration.

Treat as discovery / routing — still verify latency on the underlying host you actually use.

nodes.title: Together AI
nodes.summary: Open-model inference host.
nodes.notes: Appears as a Gemma-class host via gateways. Validate latency yourself before using for realtime.

nodes.title: OpenAI
nodes.summary: Direct API for GPT-family models; useful as a TTFT/accuracy baseline.
nodes.notes: Use as a **TTFT / accuracy baseline** when qualifying new hosts.

nodes.title: Gemma 4
nodes.summary: Strong open model for realtime voice: instruction following, tools, transfers.
nodes.notes:
- Strong **instruction following, tool use, sub-agent transfers**.
- Better accuracy than OSS models, at **higher cost per token**.
- Speed depends heavily on host — specialized fast hosts and colocated inference win.
- Smaller variants trade **cost/latency vs quality** — pick size after measuring.
- Livekit Gemma4 is 200ms TTFT

nodes.title: GPT-OSS
nodes.summary: Cheap open workhorse model; accuracy trails tuned alternatives.
nodes.notes:
Cheap on fast hosts, but **accuracy trails** tuned models like Gemma.

Keep a pre-vetted alternative for spend spikes.

nodes.title: GPT-5.6 Luna
nodes.summary: Cheaper GPT-family option for realtime agents.
nodes.notes:
- **Much cheaper tokens** than the flagship GPT tier.
- Acceptable quality/transfers, but **higher TTFT** than colocated open models.

nodes.title: GPT-5.1
nodes.summary: Expensive GPT-family baseline for latency and cost comparisons.
nodes.notes: - Use as a latency/cost **upper bound**. Keep only if the quality gap vs cheaper tiers justifies it.

nodes.title: DeepSeek-V4
nodes.summary: Flash / Pro model family available via gateways and enterprise clouds.

nodes.title: Minimax
nodes.summary: Fast model with weak tool / sub-agent reliability in voice sims.
nodes.notes:
- Unstable tool-calling 
- Lesson: **TTFT ≠ production readiness** — test tool calling + multi-agent transfers explicitly.

nodes.title: Nemotron 3
nodes.summary: Open model family; larger variants often too slow for the main voice agent.
nodes.notes: - Larger variants can be **too slow for primary voice**;

nodes.title: Muse Glimmer
nodes.summary: Open agentic model on the watchlist; claims strong published benches.
nodes.notes: Claims to beat Gemma on published benchmarks

nodes.title: Gemini Flash Lite
nodes.summary: Cheap, fast model for bulk / lighter workloads.
nodes.notes: Cheap + fast enough for batch-ish work; watch **rate limits**; confirm Vertex vs Gemini API.

nodes.title: GLM 5.x
nodes.summary: Industry latency pick for fast voice stacks.
nodes.notes: - Frequently cited for fast voice stacks (often paired with Wafer / Baseten-class hosts).

nodes.title: Inworld
nodes.summary: Cloud TTS used as a cheaper primary or failover.
nodes.notes: - Cheaper primary or failover; one provider per call, different providers across deployments.

nodes.title: Speechify
nodes.summary: Cloud TTS with good quality but a thinner accent catalog.
nodes.notes: Good quality but **thin accent catalog** — multi-provider fleets fill gaps.

nodes.title: Fish Audio
nodes.summary: Cloud TTS often cited for top voice quality, with reliability/latency tradeoffs.
nodes.notes:
- Often cited **best voice quality** with **reliability/latency tradeoffs**.
- Evaluate **emotion/prosody controls** as a quality axis beyond single-line MOS.

- Related open model path: Fish Speech (slow linguistic + fast acoustic stages, Firefly-GAN vocoder).

nodes.title: AssemblyAI
nodes.summary: Cloud ASR commonly used as a Deepgram failover.

nodes.title: Soniox
nodes.summary: Cloud ASR noted for fast endpointing.
nodes.notes: Cited as a fast endpointing option that cuts turn-taking latency.

nodes.title: Plivo
nodes.summary: Telephony / SIP carrier for voice-agent calls.
nodes.notes:
- Inbound via SIP URI; outbound termination configured at the carrier.
- **Carrier CPS limits** throttle outbound fan-out — don’t burst.
- Failures often sit at the **carrier or media layer** — document trunks + health checks.

- A waveform is the microphone signal in the time domain: amplitude changing over time.
- Working directly with it preserves the original signal, but produces a long input sequence.
- Most speech systems first turn the waveform into a time-frequency representation. That throws away some detail, but gives the model a much smaller and more useful input.
nodes.title: Audio Representation
nodes.summary: How raw microphone signal is turned into something a model can consume.

nodes.notes:
- A Fourier transform tells us which frequencies exist in a signal, but not when they occur. Speech changes constantly, so we apply it to short overlapping windows.
- Stack those windows over time and you get a spectrogram: time on one axis, frequency on the other, and energy represented by intensity.
- This is why convolutions work well on audio. A spectrogram is a grid with local patterns, much like an image.
nodes.title: Short-Time Fourier Transform
nodes.summary: Fourier analysis on short overlapping windows so frequency content can be tracked over time.

nodes.notes:
- Built by stacking STFT windows: time on one axis, frequency on the other, intensity as energy.
- Treating it as a grid is why CNN-style layers transfer so well from vision to speech.
nodes.title: Spectrogram
nodes.summary: A 2D time–frequency image of audio energy.

nodes.notes:
- Remaps frequency so small changes at low frequencies matter more than equal-sized changes at high frequencies.
- Practical default for recognition and synthesis: compact, while keeping the parts of the signal that matter for speech.
- Whisper mental model: PCM → window → FFT → mel filters + log compression → transformer.
nodes.title: Mel Spectrogram
nodes.summary: A spectrogram remapped to roughly match human hearing.

nodes.notes:
- Compress a mel spectrogram into a small feature vector. Standard input for traditional recognizers; still useful on constrained devices.
- Modern models usually learn richer representations themselves, so MFCCs are no longer the automatic choice.
nodes.title: MFCC
nodes.summary: Compact hand-designed features derived from a mel spectrogram.

nodes.notes: - A grapheme is what is written; a phoneme is a sound. TTS has to solve pronunciation, not merely read characters.
nodes.title: Phoneme
nodes.summary: A sound unit that can change a word's meaning.

nodes.notes:
- Makes pronunciation explicit. Especially useful for names, abbreviations, and languages where spelling does not map cleanly to sound.
- Byte-based models take another route: consume UTF-8 bytes and learn the mapping without a separate tokenizer or pronunciation dictionary.
nodes.title: Grapheme-to-Phoneme
nodes.summary: Converting written characters into pronunciation units.

nodes.notes:
- Useful only when it improves the signal that reaches VAD and STT. An aggressive filter can remove consonants or distort speaker cues — cleaner-sounding audio is not always better recognition input.
- RTF matters because denoising sits on every incoming frame. A model that is accurate but eats the latency budget is the wrong front-end model.
nodes.title: Denoising
nodes.summary: Cleaning incoming audio before VAD and STT.

nodes.notes:
- Turns a waveform into a compact stream of learned audio tokens and can decode those tokens back into sound. Unlike a text tokenizer, it must carry speaker identity, pitch and timing.
- Codecs make speech generation look more like language modelling: predict token IDs, then decode them into audio.
nodes.title: Neural Audio Codec
nodes.summary: Learns to turn a waveform into discrete audio tokens and back.

nodes.notes:
- Approximates a vector in stages. The first codebook picks a coarse vector; each later codebook quantizes what the earlier stages missed.
- More codebooks preserve more detail but increase bitrate and generation work — the central quality-versus-speed trade-off in codec-based speech models.
- EnCodec and Mimi are good concrete examples.
nodes.title: Residual Vector Quantization
nodes.summary: Multi-stage codebook compression used by neural audio codecs.

nodes.notes:
- Speech tokens are not all trying to preserve the same thing.
- Semantic tokens keep words and meaning (useful for ASR). Acoustic tokens keep timbre, prosody and fine sound detail (useful for generation).
- Speech-to-speech systems usually need a mixed representation. If the tokenizer drops speaker or timing information, the language model cannot recover it later.
nodes.title: Speech Tokenizer
nodes.summary: Discrete tokens for speech — semantic, acoustic, or mixed.

nodes.notes: - Built from a speech tokenizer, a language model over those tokens, and a token-to-speech synthesizer.
nodes.title: Speech Language Model
nodes.summary: An LLM that reasons over speech tokens, not only text.

nodes.notes:
- Does not need to rebuild the language model. A speech encoder turns audio into embeddings, an adapter projects them to the LLM's embedding size, and those vectors replace an audio placeholder in the prompt.
- Useful mental model: reshape speech until the LLM can attend to it like text. The encoder handles perception; the LLM handles the task.
- Temporal subsampling matters because raw audio produces far too many frames for an LLM context window.
nodes.title: Speech-Augmented LLM
nodes.summary: Project speech embeddings into an existing LLM so it can attend to audio like text.

nodes.notes: - Extracts high-level acoustic/semantic features. Often a Conformer or Whisper-style encoder, sometimes with aggressive temporal downsampling.
nodes.title: Speech Encoder
nodes.summary: Turns audio into embeddings for a speech-augmented LLM or ASR model.

nodes.notes: - Often a linear projection or a small Conformer stack. The goal is structural alignment so the LLM can treat audio embeddings like text embeddings.
nodes.title: Modality Adapter
nodes.summary: Projects speech embeddings into the LLM's token space.

nodes.notes:
- More than streaming in both directions: the model also has to decide when to yield, continue, interrupt or handle overlap.
- Half duplex is easier to operate because each turn has a clear boundary. Full duplex feels better only when interruption and timing are reliable.
nodes.title: Full Duplex
nodes.summary: Listening and speaking at the same time, including overlap and interruption.

nodes.notes:
- Gives generation a place to form a coherent answer before committing to sound.
- Easier to inspect than audio tokens, though it does not provide the clean observability of a fully cascaded pipeline.
nodes.title: Inner Monologue
nodes.summary: Predict a text-like stream before emitting acoustic tokens.

nodes.notes: - Common TTS split: text → acoustic representation → waveform. This is the first half.
nodes.title: Acoustic Model (TTS)
nodes.summary: Maps text (or phonemes) to an intermediate acoustic representation.

nodes.notes:
- Second half of the classic TTS split.
- Autoregressive waveform models such as WaveNet showed how natural neural speech could sound, but one sample at a time was too slow. Later GAN, flow and codec decoders made real-time use practical.
- HiFi-GAN is the useful baseline: fast GAN-based waveform synthesis used behind many acoustic models.
nodes.title: Vocoder
nodes.summary: Turns an acoustic representation or audio tokens into a waveform.

nodes.notes: - Useful baseline to remember for waveform synthesis speed and quality.
nodes.title: HiFi-GAN
nodes.summary: Fast GAN-based vocoder; common baseline behind many TTS systems.

nodes.notes:
- Three common levels: condition on a short reference clip, adapt the model to one speaker, or continue from recent speech context.
- Reference conditioning is convenient; adaptation usually improves fidelity but needs more clean data and a separate model or adapter.
- Evaluate intelligibility and speaker similarity separately. A sample can sound natural while sounding like the wrong person.
nodes.title: Voice Cloning
nodes.summary: Generating speech that matches a target speaker.

nodes.notes: - Usually cosine similarity of speaker embeddings. Separate from naturalness — a clone can sound good and still be the wrong voice.
nodes.title: Speaker Similarity
nodes.summary: How closely generated speech matches a target speaker embedding.

nodes.notes:
- Small enough to change the deployment calculation — practical for local or colocated TTS where a large codec language model would be wasteful.
- Treat size as an operational advantage, not proof of voice quality. Accent, pronunciation and streaming behaviour still need testing on the actual script.
nodes.title: Kokoro
nodes.summary: Small efficient TTS; useful when a large codec LM would be wasteful.

nodes.notes:
- Treats TTS as audio-token generation with a Llama-based model, then uses the SNAC codec to turn hierarchical tokens into a waveform.
- Clear example of TTS moving from spectrogram prediction toward language modelling over discrete audio.
nodes.title: Orpheus
nodes.summary: Llama-based TTS that generates audio tokens decoded by SNAC.

nodes.notes: - Hierarchical tokenization for accurate waveform reconstruction from discrete audio tokens.
nodes.title: SNAC
nodes.summary: Hierarchical neural audio codec used to decode TTS audio tokens.

nodes.notes:
- Separates slower linguistic planning from faster acoustic detail generation — meaning and waveform detail do not have to run at the same rate.
- Firefly-GAN decoder reconstructs the waveform from quantized features.
nodes.title: Fish Speech
nodes.summary: TTS with slow linguistic planning and faster acoustic detail generation.

nodes.notes: - Reconstructs waveform from Fish Speech's quantized acoustic features.
nodes.title: Firefly-GAN
nodes.summary: GAN vocoder used by Fish Speech.

nodes.notes:
- Combines a text model, reference-audio tokenizer, speaker embedding and a flow-matching acoustic generator. The reference clip conditions both who is speaking and how they speak.
- Useful example of why cloning quality depends on more than one speaker vector: reference speech can also carry rhythm and expression.
nodes.title: Chatterbox
nodes.summary: Multi-stage TTS with reference-audio conditioning for voice and style.

nodes.notes: - Encodes and decodes audio tokens for Moshi. Mixes semantic and acoustic information for real-time speech.
nodes.title: Mimi
nodes.summary: Streaming neural audio codec used by Moshi.

nodes.notes:
- Uses Mimi to encode/decode audio tokens, a language model for linguistic generation, and parallel streams for user and assistant.
- Interesting part is not just low latency: listening and speaking are concurrent streams, so overlap and interruption are part of generation rather than external pipeline logic.
- Inner text stream improves linguistic structure before audio-token generation.
nodes.title: Moshi
nodes.summary: Full-duplex speech-to-speech model with concurrent listen/speak streams.

nodes.notes:
- Built around a FastConformer encoder for transcription and speech translation.
- Aggressive temporal downsampling is the key idea: fewer audio frames while keeping enough local and global context.
- Task tokens select transcription, translation, punctuation and capitalization behaviour.
nodes.title: Canary
nodes.summary: Encoder-decoder ASR/translation model with a FastConformer encoder.

nodes.notes: - Often handled by the same encoder-decoder family as ASR, guided by task tokens.
nodes.title: Speech Translation
nodes.summary: Translating spoken language into another language's text or speech.

nodes.notes: - Covers quantization, caching, streaming, and other serving tricks. Always measure per component — STT, LLM and TTS fail differently.
nodes.title: Inference Optimization
nodes.summary: Making voice-stack inference faster, cheaper, or smaller without breaking quality.

nodes.notes:
- Reduces precision to shrink memory use and speed up inference on hardware that supports the chosen format.
- The actual win depends on the runtime and GPU. A smaller checkpoint does not automatically mean lower latency.
- Test quality per component. STT may lose rare words, an LLM may lose tool reliability, and TTS may introduce audible artefacts even when aggregate benchmarks barely move.
nodes.title: Quantization
nodes.summary: Reducing numeric precision to shrink memory and speed inference.

nodes.notes:
- Compute once for a known voice instead of re-encoding the reference clip for every utterance.
- LLM KV caching avoids recomputing the conversation prefix during token generation.
- Whole-response caching is less useful for an agent because context changes, but fixed prompts and repeated system audio can still be cached safely.
nodes.title: Speaker Embedding Cache
nodes.summary: Cache stable speaker embeddings instead of re-encoding reference audio every turn.

nodes.notes:
- Audio quality, conversation quality and business outcome are different evaluations.
- TTS: intelligibility, naturalness, speaker similarity and first-audio latency.
- STT: WER by accent, language, noise and domain vocabulary — not one overall number.
- Agent: task completion, tool correctness, interruption handling, escalation and end-to-end latency.
- A polished demo can hide failures because the room, script and caller are controlled. Keep a small set of ugly real-world calls and rerun them on every meaningful change.
nodes.title: Evaluation
nodes.summary: Measuring whether the voice agent works — by layer, not only by demo feel.

nodes.notes: - Useful for comparing signal degradation across configs. Not a substitute for human MOS on synthetic speech.
nodes.title: PESQ
nodes.summary: Automated perceptual speech quality score; useful for signal comparisons.

nodes.notes:
